title: Maternity service group antenatal care: failed first search, leads-only scan kept incomplete, two-hit second search appraised
notes: Ordinary ambiguity around a thin search. A public health midwife wants a cost-effectiveness analysis of offering group antenatal care (routing economic, explicit under both classifier rules). The first recorded search fails with HTTP 429 and records an event with status 'error' and no result count. The scan reply that follows (shape discovery) has four model leads only, one undated with null quality, and a certainty 'low': the leads are stored unverified, unknowns stay unknown, the certainty is dropped and the stage stays incomplete with the status 'leads only' (G1 to G4; A3.2). The investigator broadens the query and a second search returns only two records; the appraisal of those two records completes the stage with its own certainty and three claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. The order of the retrieved records relative to the earlier leads is not asserted (the format leaves it open); the second event's record ids are. The decision rests on c1 to c3 with both gates met on the investigator's records, and acceptance is a supported positive (accepted, ready). Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for record 1 (ev-1s02hpy) and titleYearKey hash for record 2 (ev-1426e3a). Requires D20 (leads-only scan incomplete with the certainty dropped and 'leads only' shown), S11, S13 and D5. Catches: a failed search turned into silence, certainty assigned to leads, completion without retrieval, and a thin search treated as more than it is.

inputs.need:
I am the public health midwife for a maternity service that books about 3,400 pregnancies a year across six community hubs. In January 2025 two hubs in our most deprived areas started offering group antenatal care: groups of eight to twelve women due around the same time meet for ten two-hour sessions that combine checks, education and peer support, instead of short individual appointments. Before the change, fewer than half of the women booked at those hubs attended the eight contacts we recommend, and attendance was lowest among women under 20, women new to the country and women with a previous pregnancy loss.

The trust board will decide in 2027 whether to offer group care in all six hubs. Midwives are enthusiastic, but group care needs more midwife hours per session, rooms, childcare and interpreters, and finance wants to know what it costs for each extra woman who attends her recommended contacts, and whether that is good value compared with sending reminders or offering evening clinics.

I would like to do a cost-effectiveness analysis using what we already hold: booking and attendance data for 2024 to 2026 across all six hubs, the rota and room booking data, and invoices for childcare and interpreters. I need help defining the outcome, choosing the comparison (the same hubs before 2025, the other four hubs, or both), costing the sessions properly, and presenting uncertainty honestly. I also want to know whether the evidence on group care and attendance is strong enough to rely on, because I have heard very different claims from colleagues.
inputs.constraints: No new data collection from women; existing booking, attendance, rota and invoice data only; about 60 hours of finance analyst time; the report is due to the trust board in March 2027.
localFacts: The service booked 3,412 pregnancies in 2025 across six community hubs; the two group-care hubs booked 1,086.
Group antenatal care started in the two hubs in January 2025; women booked there can choose group or individual care.
The trust's research office classified the evaluation as a service evaluation on 2026-08-05 (reference SEV-MAT-2026-21).
The finance team agreed to provide 60 hours of analyst time and 2026 unit costs for midwife hours and room hire (memo FIN-MAT-2026-09).

records.title: Group antenatal care and attendance at recommended contacts: a cluster randomised trial in 24 community clinics
records.authors: Adjei-Lindholm M, Carrasco-Whyte E, Okwuosa-Brandt L
records.abstract: We randomised 24 community clinics to offer group antenatal care or individual appointments to women booking before 16 weeks of pregnancy. Among 2,960 women, 71 percent in group-care clinics and 58 percent in individual-care clinics attended eight or more contacts (risk ratio 1.22, 95 percent confidence interval 1.09 to 1.37). The difference was larger among women under 20. Only 46 percent of women offered group care took it up. Preterm birth and low birthweight did not differ between arms. Costs were not measured, and clinics in the most deprived areas were under-represented.

records.title: Costs of group versus individual antenatal care: a micro-costing study in two maternity services
records.abstract: We micro-costed antenatal care for 412 women receiving group care and 398 receiving individual care in two maternity services. Midwife time per woman was similar, but group care required room hire, refreshments, childcare and interpreters, so the mean cost per woman was 12 percent higher (mean difference 64 in local currency). Costs per woman fell as group size rose from 8 to 12. The study did not measure attendance or outcomes, so cost-effectiveness could not be estimated. Interpreter costs varied most between the two services.

response.synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level, after a first search that failed and a leads-only reply that could not be assessed. A cluster randomised trial found that offering group care raised attendance at eight or more contacts (71 against 58 percent), especially among women under 20, with less than half of women taking up the offer. A micro-costing study found group care about 12 percent more expensive per woman, driven by rooms, childcare and interpreters and falling with larger groups. No retrieved study combines costs and attendance; the four model leads remain unchecked.
response.gradeRationale: One randomised trial with deprived areas under-represented and one costing study without outcomes; only two records, indirect to this service.
response.summary: Two retrieved records appraised; three claims; overall certainty low.

response.designSummary: Difference-in-differences for attendance and cost, combined into an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio with bootstrap uncertainty.
response.sampleSize: About 1,050 women a year book at the two group-care hubs and about 2,300 at the other four. With attendance near 50 percent, the standard error of the difference-in-differences is about 2.6 percentage points (square root of 0.25/1,050 times 2 plus 0.25/2,300 times 2), so the analysis has 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 for a difference of about 7.4 points, below the 13-point difference seen in the trial (claim c1). The cost side has no power calculation: costs are estimated with intervals.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear probability model for attendance with hub group, period and their interaction, standard errors clustered by hub; the same for cost per woman; the ratio with 2,000 bootstrap replicates resampling women within hubs, shown on a cost-effectiveness plane and an acceptability curve over a range of values the board might place on an additional attender.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Results for women under 20, women new to the country and women with a previous loss; sensitivity analyses for group size, interpreter costs and excluding the first three months of group care.
response.missingData: Women who transfer out are kept in the hub of booking up to transfer; missing invoices are reported and costed at the median.
response.multiplicity: One primary ratio; subgroup and sensitivity results descriptive.
response.software: R; code and cost inputs archived before analysis.

response.title: Offering group antenatal care in community hubs: a cost-effectiveness analysis of attendance at recommended contacts
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the incremental cost per additional woman attending eight or more antenatal contacts when community hubs offer group care. Design: cost-effectiveness analysis alongside a controlled before-after comparison of two group-care hubs and four individual-care hubs, 2024 to 2026. Results and conclusions will follow the analysis.
response.introduction: Group antenatal care can raise attendance but costs more per woman; no retrieved study combined the two. A first literature search failed and a second returned only two records, so the evidence base is thin.
response.methods: Analysis by hub of booking; difference-in-differences for attendance and cost; bootstrap uncertainty; CHEERS 2022 reporting.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present attendance and costs by hub group and period, the cost-effectiveness plane and acceptability curve, and results for three named groups.
response.discussion: The discussion will set the ratio against the board's willingness to pay and the thin evidence base.
response.limitations: Non-random hub selection; routine data; thin external evidence.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not claim effects on birth outcomes.
response.summary: CHEERS-structured draft with results left empty.
